Secondly, hepatic adenoma is a potential source of false positive imaging in suspected liver metastases as both are hypervascular and may demonstrate hypermetabolism on [18F]FDG PET (18). Furthermore, liver metastases from different types of melanoma demonstrate different levels of [18F]FDG avidity. Whereas, liver metastases from cutaneous melanoma are reliably [18F]FDG -avid (Figure 5), those from uveal melanoma show low [18F]FDG avidity resulting in false negative assessments (3). in_text_mentions: The immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells that were immune-positive for S100 protein, as seen in Figure 3. They were also positive for melanoma antigen A (Melan-A) and negative for pan-cytokeratin. The histopathological features were confirmatory of subungual melanoma of the right-sided great toe, with no evidence of lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Radiological investigations like computed tomography (CT) of the chest and ultrasonography of the whole abdomen were performed, which did not show any evidence of metastasis.

in_text_mentions: e taken from the nodule identified the diagnosis of malignant melanoma. The surgical resection of the tumor and left inguinal lymph node dissection were performed. Histological examination of the tumor revealed that atypical melanocytes proliferated larger nuclei in the epidermis and infiltrated into the dermis (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining showed that melan-A and HMB-45 were positive for tumor cells. The left inguinal lymph node metastasis was also identified. No BRAF gene mutation was detected. Based on these examinations, we diagnosed malignant melanoma with pT4bN2cM0 stage IIID.

in_text_mentions: Histology results revealed metastatic melanoma with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (Figures 5-7), stating the pathology reports were specific and in accordance with histological image findings. Flow cytometry revealed the tumor cells were exhibiting strong S100 and Sox10 positive immunostaining (Figures 8-10). The tumor cells were negative for GATA3, E-cadherin, estrogen and progesterone receptor, CD68, CD45, and broad-spectrum cytokeratin. These findings strongly support the diagnosis of metastatic melanoma of the left axilla.

panels.rationale: Single-panel low-power H&E photomicrograph (100×) from a case report of primary gingival mucosal melanoma, explicitly framed by the article title as a comparison with cutaneous melanoma. The image is a genuine patient histopathology specimen showing infiltrative proliferation of atypical melanocytic cells within the gingival mucosal stroma, with arrows marking tumor infiltration — matching the configured vocabulary finding for invasive atypical melanocytic proliferation. Prior caption triage also classified this as a keep for cutaneous_melanoma. Mucosal melanoma is a recognized less common (variant) form of melanoma; no age, ethnicity, or stage is stated in the caption or in-text mentions. [raw subtype: gingival mucosal melanoma]

panels.figure_caption: Low-power histopathologic examination of gingival mucosal melanoma. Low-power hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) photomicrograph (100×) demonstrating infiltrative growth of atypical melanocytic cells within the gingival mucosa. Arrows indicate areas of tumor infiltration.

in_text_mentions: al. On microscopy, sections from the prostate showed prostate glands with tumor infiltration and tumor cells arranged in nests and sheets. The cells were polygonal in shape with spindle nuclei containing intracellular and extracellular melanin. 6/11 lymph nodes showed metastasis. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was positive for human melanoma black 45 (HMB-45) and melan-A (Figure 4 A,B). The patient refused chemotherapy and developed pulmonary metastasis at three months. At four months, the patient succumbed to the disease from a lower respiratory tract infection, with overall survival of 6 months.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H&E section from the reported patient shows melanocytes infiltrating and disrupting the epidermis, with in-text confirmation of atypical epidermal and dermal melanocyte nests and pagetoid spread, directly supporting cutaneous melanoma. B: The panel shows PRAME-positive staining in tumor cells. PRAME is explicitly defined in the caption as preferentially expressed antigen in melanoma, and the article context and accompanying H&E support attribution to cutaneous melanoma. C: The panel shows HMB45-positive staining in tumor cells. The caption defines HMB45 as an antibody against the melanosomal gp100 protein, and the in-text IHC description supports a melanocytic melanoma diagnosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E of the patient's biopsy-proven malignant melanoma (article title and in-text confirm malignant melanoma). Shows an invasive atypical melanocytic proliferation with intracytoplasmic pigment and prominent nucleoli, curated under the configured cutaneous_melanoma key although the primary site is anorectal (mucosal). Cytology is textbook malignant melanoma. B: Immunohistochemistry of the same patient's melanoma tumor. Brown melanocytic marker staining (Melan-A +, SOX-10 +, HMB45 partial +, Vimentin +) confirms the melanocytic proliferation; the in-text explicitly flags the unusual S-100 negativity, so this is an atypical staining pattern for melanoma.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph from a case report of malignant penile melanoma. The image is a real patient photo (arrow annotation, gloved examiner) showing a large exophytic, ulcerated, heterogeneously pigmented nodular glans lesion with asymmetric growth, irregular borders, necrosis and hemorrhage, matching the caption and in-text description of advanced penile malignant melanoma (a cutaneous/mucosal melanoma manifestation). Penile melanoma is a recognized but uncommon site, so typicality is variant; stage is advanced per the caption. No ethnicity or age is stated. The visible groin/thigh skin is adequately lit and appears medium (Fitzpatrick III–IV). [raw subtype: penile melanoma]

panels.figure_caption: Histological findings of melanoma of the right breast in a male patient. (A) Core needle biopsy of the right breast shows nests of malignant tumor cells in the background of extensive melanin pigment (magnification: 100x). (B) Tumor cells demonstrate epithelioid features with nuclear pleomorphism, irregular nuclear membrane, abundant finely granular cytoplasm, and prominent large eosinophilic nuclei (magnification: 400x).
in_text_mentions: The suspicious lesion was classified as Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) category 4C - high level of suspicion (>50% to <95% likelihood of malignancy), and an ultrasound-guided biopsy was recommended. A core biopsy was performed, and the diagnosis of epithelioid-type malignant melanoma with extensive pigmentation and focal necrosis was made (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Preoperative clinical photograph of the right ventral tongue surface showing an irregular, ulcerated, raised mucosal mass. Biopsy confirmed spindle cell malignant melanoma and the lesion is untreated at presentation. Mucosal (tongue) melanoma is a recognized less-common form, hence variant typicality; white arrows annotate the lesion. [raw subtype: spindle_cell] B: Preoperative clinical photograph of the right lateral tongue surface showing the same irregular, ulcerated, raised mucosal mass indicated by white arrows. Biopsy confirmed spindle cell malignant melanoma; untreated presentation. Mucosal tongue melanoma is a recognized less-common form (variant); arrows annotate the lesion. [raw subtype: spindle_cell]
panels.attribution_text: Ozgen et al. A Rare Case of Aggressive Tongue Malignant Melanoma: Clinical Presentation and Treatment Approach.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.96184. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative tongue lesion Preoperative lesion is shown on the right ventral (A) and lateral (B) tongue surfaces. White arrows indicate the irregular and ulcerated mucosal mass on the tongue.
in_text_mentions: A 69-year-old female with a 10-year history of a tongue lesion that had recently increased in size presented to our institution. Her past medical history included hypertension and coronary artery disease. Clinical examination revealed an ulcerovegetative mass approximately 4 cm in diameter, extending from the right ventral tongue to the midline (Figures 1A, 1B). No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy or systemic findings were detected. Incisional biopsy confirmed a spindle cell subtype of malignant melanoma.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Clinical photograph of a 67-year-old patient (in-text) showing a 67 × 32 mm black macule at the umbilicus with a central 38 × 22 mm reddish nodule. The article title ('Primary umbilical malignant melanoma...'), caption and in-text all attribute this lesion to cutaneous melanoma. Asymmetry, border irregularity, color variegation and a raised amelanotic nodular component are visible, matching vocabulary findings. b: Contrast-enhanced axial CT of the same patient showing the umbilical melanoma tumor with invasion extending to the fascia, per caption and in-text (clinical diagnosis cT4bN0M0, Stage IIC). It is a real human-patient image showing a specific manifestation (local invasion) of cutaneous melanoma; the CT finding is not covered by the vocabulary and is therefore placed in proposed_findings.

in_text_mentions: At the initial presentation, physical examination revealed a 67 × 32 mm black macule with a central mass in the umbilical region with a central 38 × 22 mm erythematous nodule (Figure 1a). Whole-body computed tomography (CT) showed no obvious lymph node or visceral metastases (Figure 1b). The clinical diagnosis was cT4bN0M0, Stage IIC, and the treatment plan included primary tumor resection and sentinel lymph node biopsy. The extent of resection was determined through a preoperative conference involving dermatologists, gastrointestinal surgeons, and plastic surgeons. In accordance with the NCCN

in_text_mentions: ymph node lesion and regression of the left lung S5 lesion outside the irradiation field. This regression of the unirradiated lesion was considered the first AE (Figure 3). panels.rationale: Single-panel axial high-resolution chest CT of a human patient. The panel-specific caption identifies a left lower paracardiac lung mass that is a metastatic lesion, and the disease-focused article title ('Malignant Melanoma Presenting as Spinal Cord and Pleural Lesions') plus the in-text description of these lung lesions as metabolically active metastatic lesions (Figures 3 and 4) establish attribution to cutaneous melanoma. The in-text's 'metabolically active... denoting lung metastasis' supports the FDG-avid metastatic melanoma finding. The CT-specific appearance (paracardiac lung mass) is absent from the vocabulary and recorded as a proposed finding. Not a diagram, control, other-disease or third-party image.

panels.figure_caption: High-resolution chest CT showing another left lower lung lobe paracardiac lung mass denoting another metastatic lesion.
in_text_mentions: was continued using 9 cycles of nivolumab. Unfortunately, follow-up imaging on the 15th of July 2019 showed the development of a new metabolically active metastatic lesion in the right middle pulmonary lobe and left lower paracardiac lung lobe, and progression of the size and metabolic activity of the lesions denoting lung metastasis (Figures 3 and 4). Thus, the patient was started in ipilimumab in addition to nivolumab. The thoracic team was consulted and decided that total resection is not deemed feasible due to intraspinal extension of the primary lesion as well as multiple lung metastases.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Coronal T1WI MRI of a real patient showing a well-circumscribed sellar lesion; the disease-focused article title ('Malignant melanoma with pituitary metastasis') together with the captioned sellar manifestation attributes this to metastatic cutaneous melanoma. Best matching vocabulary finding is the MRI melanin-related metastasis entry; the sellar/pituitary site is proposed as an additional precise term. B: Coronal T2WI MRI of the same real-patient sellar lesion; disease attribution rests on the disease-focused article title plus the captioned manifestation. The lesion is a metastatic melanoma deposit in the sellar/pituitary region; T2 signal is slightly hyperintense rather than the classic melanotic hypointensity, so confidence is moderate. C: Contrast-enhanced coronal MRI showing progressive inhomogeneous enhancement of the sellar lesion, the most direct match to the vocabulary MRI metastasis finding. Attribution to metastatic...

panels.rationale: Single axial non-contrast CT of the brain showing bilateral cerebellopontine angle soft tissue masses (yellow arrows) in a 72-year-old woman with prior malignant melanoma. The in-text explicitly places metastatic melanoma in the differential for these lesions and the article title is disease-focused on prior malignant melanoma, supporting attribution to cutaneous melanoma brain metastases; bilateral CPA involvement mimicking vestibular schwannomas is a recognized but less common presentation.

in_text_mentions: The initial non-contrast CT of the brain was reported as normal. On subsequent multidisciplinary review, a soft tissue abnormality in both cerebellopontine angles was identified (Figure 1). The differential diagnosis included bilateral vestibular schwannomas and metastatic melanoma. MRI could not be performed due to the cochlear implant.

panels.rationale: Single endoscopic panel shows a non-melanotic hepatic flexure polyp; the article title and in-text confirm metastatic malignant melanoma, with biopsies positive for metastatic melanoma. The non-melanotic polypoid morphology corresponds to an amelanotic melanoma metastasis, supporting disease attribution to cutaneous melanoma. Confidence is moderate because the image is an internal metastasis rather than a primary cutaneous lesion.

in_text_mentions: a polypoid mass had been observed in the right buccal mucosa, and she had been referred to our hospital for further examination and treatment. Her relevant comorbidities included hypertension, dyslipidemia, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s performance status was 1 at the time of presentation. A biopsy was performed, and the patient was diagnosed with buccal mucosal malignant melanoma. Contrast-enhanced CT, MRI, and positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) demonstrated metastasis to the right cervical lymph nodes, resulting in a clinical stage of cT3N1M0 (Figure 1).

H&E shows invasive atypical melanocytes beneath ciliated columnar epithelium, confirming melanoma; the gross shows a black polypoid lesion. Primary nasolacrimal duct melanoma is an unusual presentation, hence atypical; mapped to the configured cutaneous_melanoma per the article disease key and prior triage. b: Inferior nasal meatus level: gross specimen (left, red line marking tumor) and H&E at x2 (middle, black arrow marking tumor) from the same patient. Histology confirms invasive melanoma beneath respiratory-type epithelium, supporting primary nasolacrimal duct origin. Unusual site/presentation; mapped to cutaneous_melanoma per article disease key and prior triage. c: Immunohistochemical stain (HMB-45) of the patient's nasolacrimal duct tumor showing diffuse cytoplasmic positivity in tumor cells, confirming...

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings confirming primary malignant melanoma of the nasolacrimal duct (a) Nasolacrimal duct level – gross appearance (left), H&E staining (×2, middle), and H&E staining (×20, right). (b) Inferior nasal meatus level – gross appearance (left) and H&E staining (×2, middle); red line indicates tumor (gross), black arrow indicates tumor (histology). A black, polypoid lesion protruding into the nasal cavity was observed. H&E staining showed atypical spindle- to polygonal-shaped cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli located beneath the ciliated columnar epithelium. The tumor was also present beneath the nasolacrimal duct mucosa, whereas the inferior nasal meatus was spared, suggesting primary origin from the nasolacrimal duct. (c-f) Immunohistochemical staining for HMB-45 (c), Melan A (d), S100P (e), and MIB-1 (f). Tumor cells were positive for HMB-45, Melan A, and S100P, with an MIB-1 labeling index of approximately 30–40%. H&E: hematoxylin and eosin

source_variants.figure_caption: Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings confirming primary malignant melanoma of the nasolacrimal duct (a) Nasolacrimal duct level – gross appearance (left), H&E staining (×2, middle), and H&E staining (×20, right). (b) Inferior nasal meatus level – gross appearance (left) and H&E staining (×2, middle); red line indicates tumor (gross), black arrow indicates tumor (histology). A black, polypoid lesion protruding into the nasal cavity was observed. H&E staining showed atypical spindle- to polygonal-shaped cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli located beneath the ciliated columnar epithelium. The tumor was also present beneath the nasolacrimal duct mucosa, whereas the inferior nasal meatus was spared, suggesting primary origin from the nasolacrimal duct. in_text_mentions: s were scheduled to monitor for signs of recurrence or metastasis and for wound care. There was a recurrence at the six-month follow-up. PET scan identified metabolically active left popliteal and external iliac lymph nodes apart from a subcentimetric subcutaneous soft tissue density nodule in the anteromedial aspect of the middle third of the left leg (Figures 6, 7). Amputation was recommended; however, the patient declined the procedure. Hence, a wide local excision was performed, and paclitaxel-carboplatin adjuvant chemotherapy was initiated. in_text_mentions: with abundant cytoplasm, fine melanin pigmentation, and pleomorphic vesicular nuclei with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, extending across all layers of the epidermis (Figure 4). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong positivity for Melan-A, HMB-45, and SOX-10 (Figure 5). in_text_mentions: ph node biopsy in October 2023. Findings included a multilobulated black subcutaneous mass. The mass was 5 x 5 x 5 cm in size. Histopathological examination of the specimen showed a spindle and epithelioid population of malignant cells with pigmentation (Figures 2-3). Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining demonstrated tumor cells positive for Melan-A (MART-1) and SRY-related HMG-box (SOX10) and negative for AE1/3 keratin, a cytokeratin. Pathological findings from the lymphatic tissue showed T cells with a decreased CD4/CD8 ratio but emphasized that this had little association with atypical cells.

in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination of the biopsy found an infiltrating malignant trabecular proliferation made of poorly differentiated epithelioid cells, with marked anisocytosis, fine and heterogeneous chromatin, and prominent nucleoli. These cells were surrounded by a polymorphic fibro-inflammatory stroma. An immunohistochemical (IHC) study found positive labeling of the tumor cells with HMB-45 (diffuse staining) and PS-100 (focal staining) antibodies and negative labeling with anti-CK7, anti-CK5/6, anti-P40, anti-AE1/AE3, and anti-CD34 antibodies (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E section of the patient's biopsy showing invasive atypical melanocytes with mitotic activity; article title confirms primary anorectal malignant melanoma and the in-text ties Figure 2A to the histopathologic diagnosis, supporting attribution to the configured melanoma disease. B: MelanA immunohistochemistry of the patient's melanoma biopsy showing positive cytoplasmic staining, confirming melanocytic lineage of the malignant cells; part of the diagnostic workup of the configured melanoma disease. C: S100 immunohistochemistry of the patient's melanoma biopsy showing diffuse positive staining of the neoplastic cells, a standard diagnostic marker for melanoma as stated in the caption and in-text. D: Ki-67 immunohistochemistry of the patient's melanoma biopsy showing nuclear positivity in about 30% of tumor cells, indicating proliferative activity of the same malignant melanoma shown in the companion H&E and IHC panels.

in_text_mentions: Biopsy histopathology confirmed malignant melanoma ( Figure 2 ). HE staining revealed disorganized tissue architecture, with neoplastic cells exhibiting enlarged, irregular nuclei, frequent mitotic figures, and uneven distribution ( Figure 2A ). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated MelanA positivity ( Figure 2B ), S100 positivity ( Figure 2C ), and Ki-67 expression in approximately 30% of tumor cells ( Figure 2D ).

in_text_mentions: wing the cytodiagnosis, the tumour board of the institute advised the patient to undergo wide local excision of the mass. The patient underwent wide local excision of the left inguinal mass, and the specimen was sent for histopathological examination. The histomorphology of the resected specimen revealed a scattered population of spindle-shaped, pleomorphic tumour cells. These cells contain scant basophilic cytoplasm with hyperchromatic nuclei containing prominent nucleoli and intracytoplasmic brown granular melanin pigment. Histological features were suggestive of metastasis of MM (Figure 5).

No third-party copyright indication. Mapped to cutaneous_melanoma per the configured vocabulary and prior caption triage (route keep); note the lesion is oral/mucosal rather than cutaneous, which lowers attribution confidence. [raw subtype: spindle cell melanoma] B: Real patient H&E (x600) captioned as spindle cell melanoma: long spindled cells with nuclear hyperchromasia, dense eosinophilic cytoplasm, cytoplasmic brown pigment and frequent mitosis, supporting invasive atypical melanocytic proliferation. No third-party copyright indication. Mapped to cutaneous_melanoma per configured vocabulary and prior triage; oral/mucular rather than cutaneous site...

panels.figure_caption: (A) and (B) Histopathology of the oral melanotic lesion. (A) Mucosa formed of stratified squamous epithelium. Subepithelium expanded by spindled cells with nuclear pleomorphism and cytoplasmic brown pigment in many cells (hematoxylin & eosin x200). (B) Long spindled cells with nuclear hyperchromasia and dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and cytoplasmic brown pigment in spindle cell melanoma. Frequent mitosis was also noted (hematoxylin & eosin x600).
in_text_mentions: Anticipating a malignant lesion, an incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. It revealed atypical melanocytes in the vertical growth phase, exhibiting cellular and nuclear pleomorphism, and an altered nuclear-cytoplasmic (NC) ratio. Long spindled cells with nuclear hyperchromasia and dense eosinophilic cytoplasm were also seen. Another feature noted was the frequent mitosis and cytoplasmic brown pigment in spindle cell melanoma. Hence, the diagnosis of malignant melanoma was established (Figures 4A, 4B).

panels.body_site: attached mandibular gingiva near left first molar (oral cavity)
panels.rationale: Preoperative intraoral clinical photograph from an article titled 'Primary Malignant Melanoma of the Mandible' showing a hyperplastic, darkly pigmented (bluish-black) melanocytic lesion on the attached mandibular gingiva adjacent to the left first molar. The lesion is a real human-patient image with a specific captioned manifestation of melanoma. It is attributed to cutaneous_melanoma as the only configured disease key and consistent with prior caption triage (route keep); however, this is an oral/mucosal presentation (a rare entity per the title), so it is treated as a variant rather than a classic cutaneous skin lesion, and confidence is moderated by the mucosal rather than strictly cutaneous site. No age or ethnicity is stated; gingival mucosa does not permit Fitzpatrick assessment. [raw subtype: primary mucosal melanoma of mandibular gingiva (oral melanoma)]

panels.figure_caption: Hyperplastic melanocytic lesion involving the first mandibular molar gingiva (preoperative picture).
in_text_mentions: Intraoral examination revealed a hyperplastic melanocytic lesion, approximately 1 cm in diameter, located in the attached mandibular gingiva near the left first molar region (Figure 1). On palpation, the lesion was firm and appeared attached to the underlying bone. There were no other visible melanocytic lesions in the oral cavity. The neck examination was unremarkable, with no visible or palpable swelling. Her past medical history was insignificant, and there was no family history of similar lesions.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a left nasal ala/nasolabial mass in a case report titled 'A Rare Presentation of Malignant Melanoma of the Face'; the in-text/caption description of a firm, pedunculated, pinkish, irregular globular swelling with crusting supports a cutaneous melanoma manifestation, most consistent with an amelanotic/nodular presentation.

in_text_mentions: On clinical examination, a 3 x 3 cm firm, pedunculated, pinkish, irregular globular swelling was seen arising from 0.5 cm inferior to the left nasal cavity over the left nasolabial fold. The left ala was pushed medially, occluding the left nasal cavity. Crusting was present over the surface of the swelling. The swelling was nontender, with no local rise in temperature and irregular margins (Figure 1). The posterior rhinoscopy was normal. The rest of the otorhinolaryngological, head and neck, and general examination were normal.

plate_findings.evidence: In-text: 'hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed numerous tumor cells of varying sizes with prominent nucleoli in the local gastric mucosal tissue, alongside some cells containing visible melanin granules (Figure 4A)'

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E histology of gastric submucosa from the index patient; in-text describes tumor cells with prominent nucleoli and visible melanin granules, and the disease-focused title ('Gastric and duodenal metastasis of malignant melanoma') attributes the metastasis to melanoma. Nests of atypical melanocytes with melanin in the submucosa match the invasive melanoma nests finding. GI metastasis is a rare (atypical) presentation. Red zoom rectangles/dashed connectors count as annotations. B: H&E histology of duodenal mucosa from the same patient; in-text identifies pigment in the localized area as characteristic of melanoma, and the article title attributes it to malignant melanoma metastasis. Pigmented atypical tumor cells in the mucosal lesion support the invasive melanoma nests finding. Duodenal metastasis is a rare (atypical) presentation. Red zoom rectangles/dashed connectors count as annotations.
panels.attribution_text: Zheng et al. Case Report: Gastric and duodenal metastasis of malignant melanoma: a rare clinical presentation.. Frontiers in oncology 2025. doi:10.3389/fonc.2025.1597380. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Stained with hematoxylin and eosin showing for (A) gastric submucosa (X 100 and X 200); (B) Duodenal mucosa (X 100 and X 200).
in_text_mentions: ng hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed numerous tumor cells of varying sizes with prominent nucleoli in the local gastric mucosal tissue, alongside some cells containing visible melanin granules ( Figure 4A ). High magnification analysis of the duodenum also identified a small quantity of pigments in the localized area, which are characteristic features of melanoma ( Figure 4B ). Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated positive expression for S100, MelanA, and SOX10 ( Figures 5A–C ), while CK and CAM5.2 the result turns out negative ( Figures 5D–F ). The Ki67 proliferation index was 90%,

panels.body_site: anorectal canal/rectum (lesion ~3.6 cm from the anal verge)
panels.rationale: Single-panel colonoscopic image of a human patient from a case report titled 'Rare primary anorectal malignant melanoma presenting with painless hematochezia.' The panel-specific caption ('a spherical, elevated lesion with an eroded surface located approximately 3.6 cm from the anal verge') plus the disease-focused article title support attribution to melanoma, and the visible flesh-colored, eroded, hemorrhagic polypoid mass corresponds to the configured cutaneous_melanoma vocabulary (raised amelanotic nodular mass; ulcerated and bleeding melanoma mass). The lesion is an anorectal mucosal melanoma, a rare and less typical presentation that was initially misattributed to rectal cancer, hence atypical typicality. No diagram, control, third-party, or other-disease element is present; the only overlays are endoscope metadata, so annotations_present is false. The image shows gastrointestinal mucosa rather than skin, nails, lips, or oral mucosa, so skin_tone is null, and the caption/in-text give no age, stage, or ethnicity information, so those fields are unknown/null. Confidence is 0.8 reflecting solid attribution of the manifestation to melanoma with the acknowledged caveat that anorectal melanoma is the mucosal rather than classic sun-exposed cutaneous subtype. [raw subtype: nodular amelanotic mucosal (anorectal)]
panels.attribution_text: Zhong et al. Rare primary anorectal malignant melanoma presenting with painless hematochezia: a case report.. Frontiers in oncology 2025. doi:10.3389/fonc.2025.1640063. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Colonoscopic image of the mass, demonstrating a spherical, elevated lesion with an eroded surface located approximately 3.6 cm from the anal verge.
in_text_mentions: rical mass ~4 cm from the anal verge, with a rough, ulcerated surface occupying half the rectal circumference; the examining glove was stained with blood upon withdrawal. Colonoscopy revealed a pedunculated polypoid lesion (~2.5 cm in diameter) near the anorectal junction, with surface erosion ( Figure 1 ). Based on the patient’s symptoms, physical examination, and colonoscopy findings, an initial diagnosis of rectal cancer was considered. The patient denied prior gastrointestinal inflammatory or neoplastic diseases, significant personal or family medical history, or relevant travel exposures.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: PET/CT panel from a patient with malignant melanoma shows FDG-avid suspected primary skin lesion and cardiac/atrial involvement, matching the FDG-avid melanoma metastasis vocabulary finding; presentation is described as unusual. B: Transesophageal echocardiogram shows tumor extending across the inter-atrial septum with aortic valve encroachment in a patient with malignant melanoma; this is a real patient image of metastatic cardiac involvement, though no exact matching vocabulary finding is available so findings are proposed.

plate_findings.evidence: in-text: metabolically active lesion involving the left mandibular first molar gingiva (SUVmax-17.6)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial fused PET-CT with an arrow marking the hypermetabolic left mandibular/gingival primary melanoma lesion; caption and in-text give SUVmax 17.6 and stage T4aN0M0. Real diagnostic patient image, not a diagram, control, or third-party image. B: Coronal whole-body PET-CT from the same study; caption states no abnormal metabolic activity elsewhere, supporting M0 staging of the mandibular/gingival melanoma. Real patient diagnostic image without a focal annotation.

in_text_mentions: ar fossa of the left lower first molar (Figure 2), with lytic erosion of the adjoining mandibular alveolus. A CECT of the chest was done, which was normal. To exclude metastasis, a positron emission tomography (PET-CECT) scan was done, which suggested a metabolically active lesion involving the left mandibular first molar gingiva (SUVmax-17.6), and there was no evidence of any metabolically active lesions elsewhere in the body (Figure 3). According to the eighth edition of the American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system for head and neck mucosal melanoma, the tumor was staged as T4aN0M0.

plate_findings.evidence: visual: nests/sheets of atypical melanocytic cells with brown melanin pigment in lung biopsy (melanoma cell nests / invasive melanocytic proliferation); caption/in-text: lung biopsy pathology supported diagnosis of malignant melanoma

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Real human lung-biopsy histopathology from the melanoma case; caption and in-text explicitly state the lung biopsy supported malignant melanoma (metastasis). Brown melanin-bearing atypical melanocytes are visible. Disease attribution strong; assignment to the nests vocabulary key uses its general synonym (melanoma cell nests) since this is metastatic, not dermal, tissue. b: Second lung-biopsy histology field; abundant coarse brown pigment within tumor cells is characteristic of melanoma and the caption/in-text attribute the lung lesion to metastatic malignant melanoma. Metastatic (non-dermal) site, so the nests key is applied via its general synonym; subtype not directly assessable from lung tissue. c: Low-power H&E of the unhealed plantar puncture-wound biopsy, i.e. the primary cutaneous site. Plantar location supports acral lentiginous melanoma (a recognized less-common form), hence variant. Microscopic biopsy, so Fitzpatrick skin...

panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a left inguinal nodular swelling in a patient whose article title identifies malignant melanoma in the groin. The panel is a real patient image and shows a raised nodular mass; no pigmentation is described, so the closest available vocabulary finding is raised amelanotic nodular melanoma, though it may represent nodal metastatic disease.

in_text_mentions: A 68-year-old male patient presented in the Outpatient Department of Surgery at the tertiary care hospital with complaints of swelling and pain over the left inguinal region for seven months. The swelling was gradually progressive and was associated with pain. The nature of the pain was dull and aching (Figure 1).
